title: Canal colonies
hookLine: new canals turned dry land green and Sikh farmers moved west to farm it

cards: Dry ground, cracked and pale, with thorny scrub and not much else. Herders cross it with their animals. Rain is rare.
Then a channel of water arrives, cut straight across the plain, and the ground on either side darkens.
Within a few seasons there is wheat where there was dust, and a family from a crowded village in central Punjab is standing in a field that, a few years before, was nobody's farm at all.

teach.b: In western Punjab, between the rivers, lay wide dry uplands that people called the bar. British engineers dug canals from the rivers across this land, and where the water went, farms could grow.
The government granted the new land to families brought in from other parts of Punjab. Sikh farmers were among them, leaving crowded home villages for bigger plots out west.
They built houses, wells and gurdwaras, and whole new villages grew up around the canals. New market towns were laid out to serve the colonies.

teach.h: A TOWN AROUND A CLOCK TOWER.
teach.b: One of them, Lyallpur, was planned with bazaars running out from a clock tower at its center. Today that city lies in Pakistan, and how Sikh families left these lands is a later, harder story.
For now, it was a story of water and wheat.
The salok at the close of the Japji names the world as a family: air is the Guru, water is the father, and the great earth is the mother.

In the colonies, farmers could watch that line take shape, water making fields out of dust. No crop grew on that plain until the water came, and a farmer's whole year hung on the canal running on time.

how: Sikh families from the old canal colonies of western Punjab still tell stories of the villages their grandparents built there, and Sikhs who recite the Japji in the morning end it with the salok that names water as the father.

games.q: you're a Sikh farmer in a crowded village in central Punjab. you're offered a bigger plot on dry land out west, where a new canal is coming. what do you do?
o: stay on your small family plot.
move west and farm the canal land.
sell your land and join the army.
games.why: Sikh farmers were among the families who moved west, building villages, wells and gurdwaras where the canals turned the bar green.

practice: Look at some water if you can, a glass on the table, a tap, rain on a window, a river from a bridge, or picture the last water you saw.

Follow it back in your mind, a reservoir, a pipe, a cloud, a river, and the fields it might have passed on the way, and let yourself feel the size of it for a moment. If you pray, say Waheguru as you look.

wordCard.voice: Canal colonies. Dry land in western Punjab, watered by new canals and settled by farming families, Sikhs among them, who built villages, wells and gurdwaras there. Today's word.
